description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Everyday Science and Scientific Applications study guide. Covers Science in Daily Life, Scientific Instruments, Units & Measurements, and Scientific Laws & Principles. Verify before formal examination use.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is everyday science?

options.A: The study of only chemical reactions in laboratories
options.B: The application of scientific principles to ordinary activities and household technologies
options.C: The study of astronomical bodies only
options.D: The study of mathematical equations only

questions.explanation: Everyday science applies principles such as mechanics, heat transfer, electricity, magnetism, optics and chemistry to ordinary activities and household technologies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a pressure cooker cook food faster?

options.A: It lowers the boiling point of water
options.B: It raises the boiling point of water above 100°C by increasing pressure
options.C: It uses microwaves to heat food
options.D: It removes all water from food

questions.explanation: Pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100°C at normal sea-level pressure, allowing food to cook at a higher temperature. The exact boiling point depends on pressure and altitude.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does steam cook food effectively?

options.B: Steam transfers energy to food and releases latent heat when it condenses on a cooler surface
options.C: Steam contains chemicals that cook food
options.D: Steam reduces the temperature of food

questions.explanation: Steam transfers energy to food; when it condenses on a cooler surface it releases latent heat, helping heat the food efficiently.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does food cook more slowly at high altitudes in an ordinary pot?

options.A: Atmospheric pressure is higher at high altitude
options.B: Atmospheric pressure is lower at high altitude, so water boils at a lower temperature
options.C: Water does not boil at high altitude
options.D: Food requires more heat at high altitude

questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure is lower at high altitude, so water boils at a lower temperature and cooking occurs at a lower temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a refrigerator cool food?

options.A: By creating cold inside the cabinet
options.B: By using a vapour-compression refrigeration system that transfers heat from the cabinet to the surroundings

questions.explanation: A vapour-compression refrigeration system circulates a refrigerant. The refrigerant evaporates in the evaporator and absorbs heat from the cabinet; it is compressed, condenses outside the cabinet and releases heat to the surroundings.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Does a refrigerator create cold?

options.B: No, it transfers heat from the insulated cabinet to the surrounding room

questions.explanation: A refrigerator does not create cold. It transfers heat from the insulated cabinet to the surrounding room using work supplied to the compressor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is the back or side of a refrigerator warm?

options.B: Because the condenser releases heat removed from the cabinet plus the energy supplied to run the compressor
options.D: Because the refrigerator creates heat instead of cold

questions.explanation: The condenser releases heat removed from the cabinet plus the energy supplied to run the compressor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of the thermostat in a refrigerator?

options.B: It senses temperature and controls the cooling system to maintain the selected temperature range

questions.explanation: The thermostat senses temperature and controls the cooling system to maintain the selected temperature range.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does an air conditioner work?

options.A: It pumps cold air from outside
options.B: Most domestic air conditioners use a refrigeration cycle to remove heat from indoor air and reject it outdoors
options.C: It adds moisture to the air
options.D: It burns fuel to produce cold air

questions.explanation: Most domestic air conditioners use a refrigeration cycle to remove heat from indoor air and reject it outdoors; they also circulate and often dehumidify indoor air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why should air-conditioner filters be cleaned?

options.A: To increase the cooling capacity beyond design limits
options.B: Clean filters maintain airflow and indoor air quality and help prevent reduced efficiency and unnecessary energy use
options.C: To make the air conditioner louder

questions.explanation: Clean filters maintain airflow and indoor air quality and help prevent reduced efficiency and unnecessary energy use.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the principle of a microwave oven?

options.A: It uses ionising radiation to heat food
options.B: Microwaves interact with polar molecules and ions in food, producing dielectric heating
options.C: It uses direct flame to heat food
options.D: It heats food by conduction only

questions.explanation: Microwaves interact with polar molecules and ions in food, producing dielectric heating. Heating is not always uniform, so standing time and stirring may be needed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Do microwave ovens make food radioactive?

options.B: No, the non-ionising microwaves heat food but do not make it radioactive
options.C: Yes, if used for too long

questions.explanation: No. The non-ionising microwaves heat food; they do not make it radioactive.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why should metal utensils generally not be used in a microwave oven?

options.B: Metal can reflect microwaves and may cause arcing or damage
options.D: Metal absorbs all microwaves without any effect

questions.explanation: Metal can reflect microwaves and may cause arcing or damage depending on shape and oven design. Only microwave-safe cookware should be used.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does an induction stove heat a vessel?

options.B: An alternating magnetic field induces electrical currents in compatible cookware, and resistance converts this energy into heat
options.C: By heating the air around the vessel

questions.explanation: An alternating magnetic field induces electrical currents in a suitable ferromagnetic or compatible cookware base; electrical resistance converts this energy into heat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does an induction cooktop need compatible cookware?

options.B: The vessel must interact effectively with the magnetic field; a magnet sticking to the base is a useful basic compatibility check
options.D: The cooktop only works with aluminium vessels

questions.explanation: The vessel must interact effectively with the magnetic field; a magnet sticking to the base is a useful basic compatibility check, though manufacturer guidance should be followed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a solar cooker work?

options.A: It uses electricity from solar panels
options.B: It captures solar radiation and converts it to heat; reflectors may concentrate sunlight, and dark vessels absorb radiation
options.C: It uses chemical reactions to cook food

questions.explanation: A solar cooker captures solar radiation and converts it to heat. Reflectors may concentrate sunlight, while dark cooking vessels absorb radiation and insulation reduces heat loss.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the limitations of a solar cooker?

options.A: It works equally well at all times
options.B: Performance depends on sunlight, weather, time of day and cooking duration; it is generally less effective at night or in heavy cloud

questions.explanation: Performance depends on sunlight, weather, time of day and cooking duration; it is generally less effective at night or in heavy cloud.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a water purifier work?

options.A: All purifiers use the same method
options.B: Different purifiers use different processes such as sediment filtration, activated carbon adsorption, membrane filtration, reverse osmosis, ultraviolet treatment or chlorination
options.D: Purifiers add minerals to water only

questions.explanation: Different purifiers use different processes, such as sediment filtration, activated carbon adsorption, membrane filtration, reverse osmosis, ultraviolet treatment or chlorination. The correct method depends on the contaminants present.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Does a UV water purifier remove dissolved salts?

options.A: Yes, it removes all dissolved salts
options.B: No, ultraviolet light inactivates susceptible microorganisms but does not remove dissolved salts or most chemical contaminants
options.C: Yes, it removes only sodium salts
options.D: UV purifiers add salts to water

questions.explanation: No. Ultraviolet light inactivates susceptible microorganisms but does not remove dissolved salts or most chemical contaminants.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Does reverse osmosis remove all contaminants?

options.A: Yes, RO removes every contaminant under all conditions
options.B: No treatment system removes every contaminant under all conditions; RO can reduce many dissolved substances but performance depends on membrane, pretreatment, maintenance and water chemistry

questions.explanation: No treatment system removes every contaminant under all conditions. RO can reduce many dissolved substances, but performance depends on membrane, pretreatment, maintenance and water chemistry.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of activated carbon in water filters?

options.B: It adsorbs many organic compounds and can reduce chlorine, taste and odour

questions.explanation: Activated carbon adsorbs many organic compounds and can reduce chlorine, taste and odour; it does not reliably remove all microbes or dissolved inorganic salts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does an electric kettle work?

options.B: Electric current passes through a resistive heating element, converting electrical energy into heat by Joule heating
options.D: It burns fuel to heat water

questions.explanation: Electric current passes through a resistive heating element, converting electrical energy into heat by Joule heating.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of an electric fuse?

options.A: It increases the current in a circuit
options.B: A fuse contains a conductor designed to melt when excessive current flows, breaking the circuit and reducing fire or equipment-damage risk

questions.explanation: A fuse contains a conductor designed to melt when excessive current flows, breaking the circuit and reducing fire or equipment-damage risk.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an MCB?

options.B: A miniature circuit breaker that automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent conditions and can generally be reset
options.C: A type of fuse that cannot be reset

questions.explanation: A miniature circuit breaker automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent conditions such as overload or short circuit and can generally be reset after the fault is corrected.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is earthing?

options.A: Connecting electrical equipment to a water pipe
options.B: Connecting exposed conductive parts of electrical equipment to earth through a protective conductor to reduce electric-shock risk
options.D: Using earth as a power source

questions.explanation: Earthing is connecting exposed conductive parts of electrical equipment to earth through a protective conductor, helping reduce electric-shock risk by providing a fault-current path.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is a three-pin plug used?

options.B: The third pin provides a protective earth connection for appliances designed with Class I protection

questions.explanation: The third pin provides a protective earth connection for appliances designed with Class I protection; live and neutral supply the circuit.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a washing machine clean clothes?

options.A: By using only water without detergent
options.B: It combines water, detergent, mechanical agitation or drum movement, rinsing and spinning
options.D: By heating clothes to high temperatures

questions.explanation: It combines water, detergent, mechanical agitation or drum movement, rinsing and spinning to remove soil and detergent from fabric.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a washing machine spin clothes?

options.B: Rapid rotation produces a centrifugal effect that drives water out through drum openings

questions.explanation: Rapid rotation produces a centrifugal effect that drives water out through drum openings, reducing moisture before drying.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a vacuum cleaner work?

options.A: It blows air to remove dust
options.B: A motor-driven fan creates a pressure difference that produces airflow, carrying dust and debris into a collection chamber
options.C: It uses water to clean surfaces

questions.explanation: A motor-driven fan creates a pressure difference that produces airflow, carrying dust and debris into a collection chamber or bag; filters retain particles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the role of an electric motor in household appliances?

options.A: It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
options.B: It converts electrical energy into mechanical motion, driving fans, pumps, compressors, mixers and washing-machine drums

questions.explanation: It converts electrical energy into mechanical motion, driving fans, pumps, compressors, mixers and washing-machine drums.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the principle of an electric fan?

options.A: It cools air by removing heat
options.B: An electric motor rotates blades that impart momentum to air, creating airflow and increasing convective heat loss from the human body
options.C: It adds moisture to the air

questions.explanation: An electric motor rotates blades that impart momentum to air, creating airflow and increasing convective heat loss from the human body.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a thermos flask reduce heat transfer?

options.A: It uses a thick layer of metal
options.B: A vacuum between walls reduces conduction and convection; reflective surfaces reduce radiation; an insulating stopper limits heat exchange through the neck
options.D: It generates heat to maintain temperature

questions.explanation: A vacuum between walls reduces conduction and convection; reflective surfaces reduce radiation; an insulating stopper limits heat exchange through the neck.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden spoon at the same temperature?

options.B: Metal conducts heat away from the hand more rapidly, so it feels colder even when both objects are at the same temperature

questions.explanation: Metal conducts heat away from the hand more rapidly, so it feels colder even when both objects are at the same temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are cooking pots often made of metal?

options.B: Metals generally conduct heat effectively and can distribute heat to food

questions.explanation: Metals generally conduct heat effectively and can distribute heat to food; handles may use insulating materials to reduce burns.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are pot handles often made of wood or heat-resistant plastic?

options.A: They conduct heat better than metal
options.B: These materials generally have lower thermal conductivity than metals and reduce heat transfer to the hand

questions.explanation: These materials generally have lower thermal conductivity than metals and reduce heat transfer to the hand.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is friction?

options.B: A force that resists relative motion or the tendency of surfaces to move relative to one another

questions.explanation: Friction is a force that resists relative motion or the tendency of surfaces to move relative to one another.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is friction useful in daily life?

options.B: It enables walking, gripping, writing, braking and transmitting motion through belts and tyres

questions.explanation: Friction enables walking, gripping, writing, braking and transmitting motion through belts and tyres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can friction be reduced?

options.B: Lubrication, polishing, using rollers or bearings, and selecting low-friction materials
options.C: By increasing the weight of objects

questions.explanation: Lubrication, polishing, using rollers or bearings, and selecting low-friction materials can reduce friction in suitable systems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do vehicle tyres have treads?

options.A: To increase the weight of the vehicle
options.B: Treads help channel water away and maintain grip in many road conditions

questions.explanation: Treads help channel water away and maintain grip in many road conditions; worn tyres can increase loss-of-control risk, especially on wet roads.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is buoyancy?

options.A: The downward force exerted by a fluid
options.B: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object partly or wholly immersed in it
options.C: The resistance of a fluid to flow
options.D: The weight of an object in air

questions.explanation: Buoyancy is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an object partly or wholly immersed in it.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a ship float although it is made of steel?

options.B: Its hollow shape makes its average density, including enclosed air, less than the density of displaced water
options.D: Water pushes ships upward due to magnetic force

questions.explanation: Its hollow shape makes its average density, including enclosed air, less than the density of the displaced water; the buoyant force balances its weight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does an object feel lighter in water?

options.B: The water exerts an upward buoyant force that reduces the object's apparent weight
options.C: The object loses mass in water
options.D: Water has no effect on weight

questions.explanation: The water exerts an upward buoyant force that reduces the object's apparent weight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are magnets used in daily life?

options.B: In speakers, motors, generators, door catches, magnetic sensors, compasses, refrigerator seals and many electronic devices

questions.explanation: Magnets are used in speakers, motors, generators, door catches, magnetic sensors, compasses, refrigerator seals and many electronic devices.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a loudspeaker produce sound?

options.B: An electrical audio signal drives a coil in a magnetic field, moving a diaphragm that produces pressure waves in air
options.D: By using static electricity to vibrate a metal plate

questions.explanation: An electrical audio signal drives a coil in a magnetic field, moving a diaphragm that produces pressure waves in air.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a microphone work?

options.B: It converts sound-induced mechanical vibrations into an electrical signal
options.C: It converts electrical signals into sound

questions.explanation: A microphone converts sound-induced mechanical vibrations into an electrical signal, using technologies such as dynamic, condenser or electret mechanisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are lenses used in daily life?

options.B: In spectacles, cameras, microscopes, telescopes and projectors to refract light and form or modify images

questions.explanation: Lenses in spectacles, cameras, microscopes, telescopes and projectors refract light to form or modify images.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of a convex lens?

options.B: It converges parallel rays in the paraxial approximation and can form real or virtual images depending on object position

questions.explanation: A convex lens converges parallel rays in the paraxial approximation and can form real or virtual images depending on object position.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of a concave lens?

options.B: It diverges parallel rays and usually forms a virtual, erect and diminished image for a real object
options.D: It has no effect on light

questions.explanation: A concave lens diverges parallel rays and usually forms a virtual, erect and diminished image for a real object.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a camera form an image?

options.B: A lens focuses light onto a photosensitive sensor or film; aperture, shutter time and sensitivity influence exposure

questions.explanation: A lens focuses light onto a photosensitive sensor or film; aperture, shutter time and sensitivity influence exposure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a periscope work?

options.A: It uses lenses to magnify objects
options.B: It uses mirrors or prisms to redirect light, allowing an observer to see over or around an obstruction
options.C: It uses sound waves to detect objects
options.D: It uses magnets to bend light

questions.explanation: It uses mirrors or prisms to redirect light, allowing an observer to see over or around an obstruction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does a simple electric circuit work?

options.B: A source provides potential difference; a closed conducting path allows current to flow through components that transfer electrical energy

questions.explanation: A source provides potential difference; a closed conducting path allows current to flow through components that transfer electrical energy.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electrical power in a household appliance?

options.A: The total energy stored in the appliance
options.B: The rate at which electrical energy is transferred or converted
options.D: The voltage supplied to the appliance

questions.explanation: Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred or converted. For a DC circuit, P = VI; for AC systems, real power depends also on power factor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does one kilowatt-hour mean?

options.A: The energy used by a 1 W device for one hour
options.B: The energy used by a 1 kW device operating for one hour; it equals 3.6 million joules
options.C: The power of a 1 kW device
options.D: The voltage of a household circuit

questions.explanation: The energy used by a 1 kW device operating for one hour; it equals 3.6 million joules.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can households conserve electricity?

options.A: By keeping all appliances on standby
options.B: By using efficient appliances and LED lighting, switching off unused devices, choosing appropriate cooling settings, maintaining equipment and improving insulation

questions.explanation: Use efficient appliances and LED lighting, switch off unused devices, choose appropriate cooling settings, maintain equipment, improve insulation and avoid standby consumption where practical.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are LED lamps more efficient than incandescent lamps?

options.B: LEDs convert a larger share of electrical energy into visible light and generally produce less waste heat for the same light output
options.D: LEDs have no advantage over incandescent lamps

questions.explanation: LEDs convert a larger share of electrical energy into visible light and generally produce less waste heat for the same light output.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is standby power?

options.A: Power used when the device is fully on
options.B: Electricity consumed by equipment while it is switched off or in standby mode but remains connected to the supply

questions.explanation: Standby power is electricity consumed by equipment while it is switched off or in standby mode but remains connected to the supply.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a pressure cooker need its safety valve and gasket?

options.B: They regulate pressure and provide sealing and pressure-release functions
options.D: To reduce the boiling point of water

questions.explanation: They regulate pressure and provide sealing and pressure-release functions. Never block the vent or tamper with safety components.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does water boil at a lower temperature at high altitude?

options.A: Because water is different at high altitude
options.B: Lower atmospheric pressure reduces the boiling temperature at which water's vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure
options.D: Because the water contains more oxygen

questions.explanation: Lower atmospheric pressure reduces the boiling temperature at which water's vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does evaporation cause cooling?

options.A: Evaporation adds heat to the liquid
options.B: Higher-energy molecules escape from a liquid surface, reducing the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid
options.C: Evaporation increases the temperature of the liquid
options.D: Evaporation has no effect on temperature

questions.explanation: Higher-energy molecules escape from a liquid surface, reducing the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a wet cloth feel cool in moving air?

options.A: Moving air adds heat to the cloth
options.B: Airflow speeds evaporation, which removes latent heat from the cloth and nearby surface
options.C: Moving air reduces the temperature of the cloth directly

questions.explanation: Airflow speeds evaporation, which removes latent heat from the cloth and nearby surface.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do we see lightning before hearing thunder?

options.B: Light travels vastly faster than sound, so the flash reaches an observer before the sound wave
options.C: Thunder is produced later than lightning

questions.explanation: Light travels vastly faster than sound, so the flash reaches an observer before the sound wave.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does a metal object become hot when current passes through it?

options.B: Electrical resistance converts electrical energy into heat, described by Joule heating
options.D: Because metals absorb heat from the surroundings

questions.explanation: Electrical resistance converts electrical energy into heat, described by Joule heating.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the principle behind an electric generator?

options.B: Electromagnetic induction: changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an electromotive force

questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction: changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an electromotive force.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a motor and a generator?

options.B: A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy; a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
options.C: A motor converts mechanical energy into electrical energy; a generator converts electrical energy into mechanical energy

questions.explanation: A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy; a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a thermometer measure?

options.B: Temperature

questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature. Common types include liquid-in-glass, digital, thermocouple and infrared thermometers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a barometer measure?

options.B: Atmospheric pressure

questions.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; mercury and aneroid barometers are traditional types.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a hygrometer measure?

options.B: Humidity, especially relative humidity

questions.explanation: A hygrometer measures humidity, especially relative humidity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a hydrometer measure?

options.B: The relative density or specific gravity of liquids by floating at a depth determined by liquid density

questions.explanation: A hydrometer measures the relative density or specific gravity of liquids by floating at a depth determined by liquid density.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a lactometer used for?

options.B: Estimating the density or specific gravity of milk; it does not by itself prove milk purity or detect every adulterant
options.C: Measuring the fat content of milk

questions.explanation: A lactometer is a type of hydrometer used to estimate the density or specific gravity of milk; it does not by itself prove milk purity or detect every adulterant.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an ammeter measure?

options.B: Electric current

questions.explanation: An ammeter measures electric current and is connected in series in an ideal circuit; practical ammeters have low resistance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a voltmeter measure?

options.B: Potential difference between two points and is connected in parallel

questions.explanation: A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points and is connected in parallel; practical voltmeters have high resistance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a galvanometer do?

options.B: Detects or measures small electric currents and their direction

questions.explanation: A galvanometer detects or measures small electric currents and their direction; some types can be adapted into ammeters or voltmeters.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an ohmmeter measure?

options.B: Electrical resistance

questions.explanation: An ohmmeter measures electrical resistance, generally using an internal source; resistance should normally be measured with the circuit de-energised and isolated.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a multimeter?

options.A: An instrument that measures only voltage
options.B: A device that combines functions such as measuring voltage, current and resistance; some models also measure continuity, capacitance, frequency or temperature
options.C: An instrument that measures only resistance
options.D: A device that measures only current

questions.explanation: A multimeter combines functions such as measuring voltage, current and resistance; some models also measure continuity, capacitance, frequency or temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an anemometer measure?

options.B: Wind speed

questions.explanation: An anemometer measures wind speed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a rain gauge measure?

options.B: The amount of precipitation collected over a defined period

questions.explanation: A rain gauge measures the amount of precipitation collected over a defined period.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a seismograph record?

options.B: Ground motion; the recorded trace is called a seismogram

questions.explanation: A seismograph records ground motion; the recorded trace is called a seismogram.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an altimeter measure?

options.B: Altitude, commonly by using atmospheric pressure or satellite positioning

questions.explanation: An altimeter measures altitude, commonly by using atmospheric pressure or satellite positioning.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a speedometer indicate?

options.B: The instantaneous speed of a vehicle

questions.explanation: A speedometer indicates the instantaneous speed of a vehicle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an odometer record?

options.B: The cumulative distance travelled by a vehicle

questions.explanation: An odometer records the cumulative distance travelled by a vehicle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a microscope do?

options.B: Uses lenses or other optical/electronic systems to magnify or resolve small objects

questions.explanation: A microscope uses lenses or other optical/electronic systems to magnify or resolve small objects.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a telescope do?

options.B: Collects and focuses electromagnetic radiation to observe distant objects

questions.explanation: A telescope collects and focuses electromagnetic radiation to observe distant objects; optical telescopes use visible light.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a periscope used for?

options.B: Viewing objects from a position with an obstructed direct line of sight using mirrors or prisms

questions.explanation: A periscope uses mirrors or prisms to view objects from a position with an obstructed direct line of sight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a stethoscope used for?

options.B: Listening to internal body sounds, especially heart and lung sounds

questions.explanation: A stethoscope allows healthcare professionals to listen to internal body sounds, especially heart and lung sounds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a sphygmomanometer measure?

options.B: Blood pressure, traditionally using an inflatable cuff and pressure gauge

questions.explanation: A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure, traditionally using an inflatable cuff and pressure gauge; automated versions use electronic sensors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an ECG machine record?

options.B: Electrical activity of the heart from electrodes placed on the body

questions.explanation: An ECG machine records electrical activity of the heart from electrodes placed on the body; it is used to assess heart rhythm and related patterns.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does an EEG machine record?

options.B: Electrical activity of the brain using electrodes placed on the scalp

questions.explanation: An EEG machine records electrical activity of the brain using electrodes placed on the scalp.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a Geiger counter detect?

options.B: Ionising radiation using a Geiger-Muller tube

questions.explanation: A Geiger counter detects ionising radiation using a Geiger-Muller tube; readings depend on radiation type, energy and instrument calibration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a spectroscope do?

options.B: Separates light into its component wavelengths to study spectra and identify features of emitted or absorbed radiation

questions.explanation: A spectroscope separates light into its component wavelengths to study spectra and identify features of emitted or absorbed radiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a calorimeter measure?

options.B: Heat transferred or released in a physical or chemical process

questions.explanation: A calorimeter measures heat transferred or released in a physical or chemical process.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a manometer measure?

options.B: Pressure, often pressure difference between a gas and a reference pressure, using a liquid column or sensor

questions.explanation: A manometer measures pressure, often pressure difference between a gas and a reference pressure, using a liquid column or sensor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a potentiometer?

options.A: A device that measures atmospheric pressure
options.B: A variable voltage divider; in classical measurement it can compare or measure potential difference accurately with negligible current drawn at balance
options.D: A device that measures wind speed

questions.explanation: A potentiometer is a variable voltage divider; in classical measurement it can compare or measure potential difference accurately with negligible current drawn at balance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does a spectrophotometer measure?

options.B: How much light a sample absorbs or transmits at selected wavelengths

questions.explanation: A spectrophotometer measures how much light a sample absorbs or transmits at selected wavelengths.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument measures the density of a liquid?

options.B: Hydrometer

questions.explanation: A hydrometer can estimate liquid density or specific gravity; a lactometer is a specialised hydrometer for milk.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument measures small current?

options.B: Galvanometer

questions.explanation: A galvanometer is used to detect or measure small currents.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument records heart electrical activity?

options.B: ECG or EKG machine

questions.explanation: An electrocardiograph (ECG or EKG) machine records heart electrical activity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument records brain electrical activity?

options.B: EEG machine

questions.explanation: An electroencephalograph (EEG) machine records brain electrical activity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument records earthquake vibrations?

options.B: Seismograph

questions.explanation: A seismograph records earthquake vibrations; its output is a seismogram.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument measures wind direction?

options.B: Wind vane

questions.explanation: A wind vane measures wind direction; an anemometer measures wind speed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instruments measure vehicle distance and speed?

options.B: Odometer measures distance travelled; speedometer indicates speed

questions.explanation: An odometer measures distance travelled; a speedometer indicates speed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a microscope and a telescope?

options.A: Both are used for the same purpose
options.B: A microscope is designed to resolve small nearby objects; a telescope collects radiation from distant objects
options.C: A microscope observes distant objects; a telescope magnifies small objects

questions.explanation: A microscope is designed to resolve small nearby objects; a telescope collects radiation from distant objects.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a barometer and a manometer?

options.B: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; a manometer commonly measures pressure or pressure difference in a fluid system
options.C: A barometer measures temperature; a manometer measures pressure

questions.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; a manometer commonly measures pressure or pressure difference in a fluid system.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between an ECG and an EEG?

options.B: ECG records the heart's electrical activity; EEG records electrical activity of the brain
options.C: ECG records brain activity; EEG records heart activity

questions.explanation: ECG records the heart's electrical activity; EEG records electrical activity of the brain.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between an ammeter and a voltmeter in terms of connection?

options.B: An ammeter is connected in series; a voltmeter is connected in parallel
options.C: An ammeter is connected in parallel; a voltmeter is connected in series

questions.explanation: An ammeter is connected in series and has low resistance; a voltmeter is connected in parallel and has high resistance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI system?

options.A: A system of measurement based on three base units
options.B: The International System of Units based on seven base units and defined derived units
options.C: A system used only in the United States
options.D: A system based on the imperial units

questions.explanation: The International System of Units (SI) is the internationally agreed system of measurement based on seven base units and defined derived units.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How many SI base quantities are there?
questions.explanation: There are seven SI base quantities: length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of length?

options.B: Metre

questions.explanation: The SI unit of length is the metre (m).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of mass?

options.B: Kilogram

questions.explanation: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of time?

options.B: Hour

questions.explanation: The SI unit of time is the second (s).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of temperature?

options.B: Fahrenheit

questions.explanation: The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K). Degree Celsius (°C) is also accepted for many everyday temperature measurements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?

options.B: Ampere

questions.explanation: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of amount of substance?

options.B: Mole

questions.explanation: The SI unit of amount of substance is the mole (mol).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of luminous intensity?

options.B: Lux

questions.explanation: The SI unit of luminous intensity is the candela (cd).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?

options.B: Watt

questions.explanation: The SI unit of force is the newton (N), equal to kg·m·s⁻².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of work and energy?

options.B: Joule

questions.explanation: The SI unit of work and energy is the joule (J), equal to N·m or kg·m²·s⁻².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of power?

options.B: Newton

questions.explanation: The SI unit of power is the watt (W), equal to J/s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?

options.B: Joule

questions.explanation: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), equal to N/m².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric charge?

options.B: Coulomb

questions.explanation: The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C), equal to A·s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of potential difference?

options.B: Coulomb

questions.explanation: The SI unit of potential difference is the volt (V), equal to J/C.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of resistance?

options.B: Ampere

questions.explanation: The SI unit of resistance is the ohm (Ω), equal to V/A.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of frequency?

options.B: Hertz

questions.explanation: The SI unit of frequency is the hertz (Hz), equal to s⁻¹.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of sound intensity?

options.B: Watt per square metre

questions.explanation: The SI unit of sound intensity is watt per square metre (W/m²). Sound intensity level is commonly expressed in decibels (dB), a logarithmic, dimensionless level.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of radioactive activity?

options.B: Sievert

questions.explanation: The SI unit of radioactive activity is the becquerel (Bq), equal to one nuclear transformation per second.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of absorbed radiation dose?

options.B: Gray

questions.explanation: The SI unit of absorbed radiation dose is the gray (Gy), equal to one joule per kilogram.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of equivalent or effective radiation dose?

options.B: Becquerel

questions.explanation: The SI unit of equivalent or effective radiation dose is the sievert (Sv), which accounts for radiation type and, for effective dose, tissue sensitivity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of heat?

options.B: Joule

questions.explanation: The SI unit of heat is the joule (J), because heat is energy transferred due to temperature difference.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of density?

options.B: kg/m³

questions.explanation: The SI unit of density is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m³).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of volume?

options.B: Cubic metre

questions.explanation: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre (m³); litre (L) is accepted for use with SI.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of area?

options.B: Cubic metre

questions.explanation: The SI unit of area is the square metre (m²).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric capacitance?

options.B: Farad

questions.explanation: The SI unit of electric capacitance is the farad (F).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of inductance?

options.B: Henry

questions.explanation: The SI unit of inductance is the henry (H).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?

options.B: Weber

questions.explanation: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density?

options.B: Henry

questions.explanation: The SI unit of magnetic flux density is the tesla (T).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of luminous flux?

options.B: Lumen

questions.explanation: The SI unit of luminous flux is the lumen (lm).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of illuminance?

options.B: Candela

questions.explanation: The SI unit of illuminance is the lux (lx), equal to lumen per square metre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of angle?

options.B: Radian

questions.explanation: The SI unit of angle is the radian (rad); the solid-angle unit is steradian (sr).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the value of standard gravity?
questions.explanation: The conventional standard acceleration of gravity is 9.80665 m/s²; local gravitational acceleration varies with latitude, altitude and geology.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the speed of light in vacuum?
questions.explanation: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second (m/s).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the value of the elementary charge?
questions.explanation: The elementary charge is exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb in the SI definition.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the value of the Planck constant?
questions.explanation: The Planck constant is exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-second (J·s) in the SI definition.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the value of Avogadro's constant?
questions.explanation: Avogadro's constant is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ in the SI definition.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate value of the universal gas constant?

options.B: 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹

questions.explanation: The universal gas constant is approximately 8.314462618 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate value of the gravitational constant?
questions.explanation: The gravitational constant is approximately 6.67430 × 10⁻¹¹ J·m²·kg⁻¹·s⁻²; it is measured experimentally and has uncertainty.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is absolute zero?

options.B: 0 K, equal to -273.15°C

questions.explanation: Absolute zero is 0 K, equal to -273.15°C; it is the lower limit of thermodynamic temperature.

questions.question: How do you convert centimetres to metres?

questions.question: How do you convert grams to kilograms?

questions.question: What is one bar in pascals?

questions.question: What is one calorie in joules?
questions.explanation: The thermochemical calorie is 4.184 J; food Calories (kilocalories) are 1,000 small calories.

options.B: A method of checking physical equations and relationships by comparing dimensions such as mass, length and time on both sides

questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis is a method of checking physical equations and relationships by comparing dimensions such as mass, length and time on both sides.

questions.question: What are the dimensions of velocity?
